claims.text: Employment means doing paid work: a person of working age who works for pay, or who holds a job and is away from it briefly, is employed; the labour force is made up of the employed together with the unemployed, those seeking work.

claims.text: Full employment is a state where unemployment has fallen to the level that remains when the economy is working at capacity: people still move between jobs and skills still take time to match posts, so full employment does not mean an unemployment rate of zero.

claims.text: Retirement is not unemployment: a retiree has left the labour force at the end of a working life and is not seeking work, whereas a person counted unemployed is seeking work and able to start it - the test that separates them is whether the person is actively seeking and available for work.

claims.text: Cyclical unemployment and structural unemployment differ in their cause and their length: cyclical unemployment comes from a fall in total spending across the economy and tends to fall back when spending recovers, whereas structural unemployment comes from a lasting change in what the economy makes or how it makes it and tends to persist after spending recovers; the test that tells them apart is what caused the job loss and whether the jobs return with the next recovery.

claims.text: The pattern of employment is the split of the employed across sectors, occupations and regions, and between public and private and formal and informal work; as an economy develops, the share of workers in primary work tends to fall and the share in tertiary work tends to rise, a movement Namibia has shared since independence and Brazil lived in its shift from farms to cities.

claims.text: As household incomes rise, a smaller share of spending goes on food and farm goods and a larger share goes on services, so tertiary jobs tend to grow faster than farm jobs; changing social attitudes and wider schooling have raised the proportion of women in paid work, in Namibia as in Japan, where the share of women in the labour force rose steadily over recent decades.

claims.text: As a country moves towards a market economy, the proportion of workers employed in the public sector tends to fall, because state-owned firms are reduced, sold or reorganised and private firms take on more of the hiring, a movement Vietnam's state enterprises lived through as private workshops took workers on.

claims.text: The claimant count measures unemployment by counting the people registered as seeking work and claiming government support for the unemployed; it is gathered from benefit records, so it is quick to produce, and it tends to miss job seekers who cannot claim support or do not register.

claims.text: A labour force survey measures unemployment by asking a sample of households about their work in a fixed week: a person is counted unemployed who was without paid work, was available to start and had sought work recently, so the survey reaches seekers the benefit records do not.

claims.text: Frictional unemployment is the short-term unemployment of people moving between jobs: a student leaving college takes weeks to find a first post, and at any moment some people are in that gap, which is why frictional unemployment persists in a well-run economy.

claims.text: Structural unemployment arises when a lasting change removes the need for particular work: machines replace hand tasks, a product is displaced by a new one, or the skills workers hold no longer match the skills employers seek, and the jobs lost do not tend to return when spending recovers, so the workers affected often need retraining or a move to new work.

claims.text: Cyclical unemployment arises when total spending across the economy falls in a downturn: firms sell less, cut output and lay workers off, and the jobs tend to return as spending recovers, which is what gives this type its name.

claims.text: For the individual, unemployment tends to cut income and raise the risk of poverty: a jobless worker loses the wage that paid for food, school fees and rent, and skills fade while work is missed, so the longer the spell lasts, the harder returning to work tends to become.

claims.text: For firms, unemployment tends to hold back sales: households without wages spend less, so orders fall across the shops and suppliers they used to buy from, even as a larger pool of job seekers makes hiring easier.

claims.text: For the economy as a whole, unemployment means output lost: the goods and services the jobless could have produced go unmade, tax revenue falls while spending on support rises, which strains the budget, and skills fading over long spells lower what the economy can produce.

claims.text: A cause of unemployment is what produces it - a fall in spending, a closure, a new machine - whereas a consequence is what unemployment produces - lost income, weaker sales, lost output; the direction of the arrow separates them, and the test is to ask which way the effect runs: toward unemployment, or away from it.

claims.text: Policies to reduce unemployment are government measures intended to raise the number of people in work, and the range works through two doors: demand-side measures that lift total spending so firms sell more and take on staff, and supply-side measures that make job seekers more employable and hiring easier.

claims.text: Where unemployment comes from weak spending, measures that lift total spending tend to create work: building projects put job seekers directly onto sites, tax cuts leave households with more to spend, and where the economy has spare capacity, the extra income earned is spent again, so further hiring follows; the jobs last as long as the demand does.
